text: Every qubit amplitude you will ever compute is a complex number, and Python has a complex number type built into the language itself, no import required. This lesson is the toolkit for writing, combining, and interpreting complex numbers before NumPy enters the picture.

Python uses j, not i, as the imaginary unit suffix, and complex is a native type alongside int and float. You'll add and multiply complex numbers, flip the imaginary part's sign with dot conjugate, and take the modulus with abs, the distance from the origin. cmath dot polar and cmath dot rect convert between rectangular and polar form. And abs of an amplitude, squared, is exactly the arithmetic that becomes a measurement probability.

Adding three plus four j and one minus two j gives four plus two j, adding real and imaginary parts separately. Multiplying them gives eleven minus two j, using the distributive rule with j squared equals negative one. The conjugate of three plus four j flips to three minus four j. And the modulus, abs of three plus four j, is five point zero, a three-four-five right triangle in disguise.

For the state one over root two times ket-zero plus j ket-one, the two amplitudes are complex numbers, and squaring their moduli gives the measurement probabilities. Each one comes out to zero point four nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine, not a perfectly clean zero point five, because s itself is already a rounded floating-point value before it's even squared. Adding both probabilities gives zero point nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine nine eight, not exactly one — a real, reproducible floating-point gap.
Next lesson turns unitary and Hermitian, the two defining properties of quantum gates and observables, into a few lines of NumPy you can run against any matrix.
